title: Introduction
introduction: Network Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) serve as critical security components for identifying potentially malicious network activities (Denning, 1987). This study presents a comparative analysis of machine learning techniques for binary classification of network traffic using the NSL-KDD benchmark dataset.

sections.title: Background and Problem Statement
sections.content_html:
Traditional signature-based intrusion detection systems fail against zero-day exploits and novel attack vectors. Machine learning offers an alternative by enabling systems to learn patterns from data and generalize to detect previously unseen attack variants (Buczak & Guven, 2016).

The NSL-KDD dataset (Tavallaee et al., 2009) addresses limitations of the original KDD Cup 1999 dataset by removing duplicate records. It contains 125,973 training instances with 41 features (expanding to 121 after encoding), partitioned into DoS, Probe, R2L, and U2R attack categories.

Key Challenges: Class imbalance (53.46% attacks in training, 56.98% in test), novel attack detection (test set includes attack types absent from training), and appropriate evaluation metrics for imbalanced datasets.

sections.title: Research Objectives
sections.content_html:
This study pursues the following objectives:

  1. Compare representative classifiers from three algorithm families—ensemble methods (BaggingClassifier), non-linear methods (DecisionTreeClassifier), and support vector methods (RidgeClassifier)
  2. Apply systematic hyperparameter optimization using 5-fold cross-validation
  3. Assess performance using Balanced Accuracy, MCC, and Attack Detection Rate
  4. Conduct bias-variance decomposition to characterize error sources
  5. Provide practical recommendations for ML-based intrusion detection

Scope: Binary classification (normal vs. attack) using supervised learning on NSL-KDD.

sections.title: Literature Review
sections.content_html:
The foundations of intrusion detection trace to Anderson (1980) and Denning (1987). Decision Trees (Quinlan, 1986; Breiman et al., 1984) achieve competitive accuracy while producing interpretable rule sets. Ahmad et al. (2018) demonstrated that tree-based methods consistently outperform linear classifiers on NSL-KDD.

Ensemble Methods (Breiman, 1996, 2001) combine multiple classifiers to reduce variance. Aburomman & Reaz (2017) surveyed ensemble approaches for IDS. Support Vector Methods (Cortes & Vapnik, 1995) find optimal separating hyperplanes; however, effectiveness depends on linear separability.

Recent surveys by Thakkar & Lohiya (2023) advocate for MCC and balanced accuracy over simple accuracy for imbalanced datasets. Matthews Correlation Coefficient has emerged as the preferred metric (Matthews, 1975; Chicco & Jurman, 2020).

Research Gap: Few studies provide systematic bias-variance decomposition alongside traditional metrics. This study addresses this gap by combining multi-metric evaluation with bootstrap-based bias-variance analysis.

sections.title: Overview of Machine Learning Models
sections.content_html:
Three team members independently investigated different algorithm families:

Muhammad Usama Fazal (TP086008) - BaggingClassifier: Bootstrap Aggregating with 150 decision tree estimators. Reduces variance through majority voting. Configuration: 85% max sample ratio, balanced class weights.

Md Sohel Rana (TP086217) - DecisionTreeClassifier: Recursively partitions feature space using Gini impurity. Provides interpretable decision rules with O(log n) prediction complexity. Configuration: max_depth=20.

Imran Shahadat Noble (TP087895) - RidgeClassifier: L2-regularized least squares classification. Assumes linear separability. Configuration: balanced class weights, default regularization.

sections.title: Document Structure
sections.content_html: Chapter 2 details methodology including data preprocessing and evaluation metrics. Chapter 3 presents results with bias-variance analysis. Chapter 4 describes individual contributions. Chapter 5 concludes with recommendations.
